Sourced Statements: Smoke from fires burning in Florida and Georgia was pushing into the Appalachian Mountains and into parts of West Virginia on Friday, and forecasters said it could reach as far as the southern parts of Pennsylvania and Ohio.

Andy Snyder, a fire meteorologist with the U.S. Wildland Fire Service, said the smoke was likely to continue for days, with the acrid air drifting as the winds shift and the fires continue to burn through a landscape that severe drought has left dry and flammable.
Title of Source: Fire meteorologist, U.S. Wildland Fire Service

Sourced Statements: Rich Bann, a meteorologist with the Weather Prediction Center, said concentrations on Friday were likely to remain low.
“It might just be a little hazier than usual,” he said.
The largest, the 30,000-acre Pineland Road fire in Georgia, “has been the major source of the smoke,” Mr. Snyder said.
Title of Source: Fire meteorologist, U.S. Wildland Fire Service

Sourced Statements: The National Weather Service office serving Atlanta warned that the air quality in the area could be unhealthy for people who are sensitive to ozone and smoke.
The storms are unlikely to bring enough rain to extinguish the fires, which have probably burned under the surface and deep into the organic soil, Mr. Snyder said.
Title of Source: Fire meteorologist, U.S. Wildland Fire Service

Sourced Statements: “They're expecting these to be long-term fires,” he said.

Sourced Statements: It’s considered “super fog” by meteorologists when visibility levels drop below 10 feet, leading to dangerous conditions on roads.
“You can go from perfect visibility to zero feet in a very short distance,” Mr. Snyder said.
Title of Source: Fire meteorologist, U.S. Wildland Fire Service
